title: Swedish government blocks ChatGPT and Claude. Here's why
content:
The ban on employees using browser-based versions of ChatGPT and Claude took effect on Monday 26 October amid security concerns over data processing.
Swedish government employees can no longer use browser-based versions of OpenAI’s ChatGPT or Anthropic’s Claude on their work computers following security concerns relating to the processing of sensitive data.
The decision comes following a review of AI tools used by workers at the Swedish Transport Administration earlier this year that found “problematic” uses of the AI platforms in carrying out government work.
Officials were concerned that entering sensitive information into these models without an agreement setting out how to protect and secure the data could lead to it being fed into the model and stored for training.
The use of platforms not regulated or protected by such agreements, also known as shadow IT, could bring “consequences for our information security”, said Mikael Wettercrantz, director of digitalisation at the Government Offices of Sweden.
Microsoft’s Copilot, which has passed a security screening process and is covered by a security agreement between the US company and the Swedish government, is being recommended as an alternative.
While government workers will still be able to use AI to help them carry out their tasks, they will do so under tighter security controls and with just a limited number of employees permitted to continue using ChatGPT and Claude but only through a special platform for AI assistants developed by Swedish authorities.
According to the Swedish public broadcaster Sveriges Radio, restrictions on the use of ChatGPT and Claude have also been put in place at the Swedish Tax Agency and the National Board of Institutional Care. The Swedish Enforcement Authority is currently reviewing the issue.
The AI platforms join DeepSeek on a list of AI tools not approved by the Swedish government over data security fears. Last week, the US announced it was banning all products and services from the Chinese AI company.

report.summary: Sweden barred government workers from browser-based ChatGPT and Claude over sensitive data security, recommending Microsoft Copilot under a secured agreement.
report.background: Governments are trying to capture generative AI's productivity gains without exposing sensitive public-sector data. Browser-based chatbots are easy to adopt, but when employees paste citizen, legal, or operational information into tools not covered by a data-processing agreement, that data may be stored or used for model training. Sweden's decision follows a review of AI use at the Swedish Transport Administration earlier this year that found problematic practices. The ban reflects a broader public-sector push against 'shadow IT' and toward approved enterprise AI tools with clear security terms, auditability, and data controls. It also fits a wider European pattern of agencies treating AI procurement as a security and compliance issue, not just a technology choice.
key_points: The ban covers browser-based ChatGPT and Claude on Swedish government work computers and took effect on 26 October. It does not eliminate AI use entirely: a limited number of employees may still access the tools through a special Swedish government AI-assistant platform with tighter controls.

The trigger was a review of AI tools at the Swedish Transport Administration, which found problematic uses of the platforms for government work. Officials feared sensitive information entered without a data-protection agreement could be fed into models and stored for training.

Microsoft Copilot is the recommended alternative because it passed a security screening and is covered by a security agreement between Microsoft and the Swedish government. That makes it the approved path for everyday AI assistance.

The restrictions extend beyond the central government. Sweden's Tax Agency and National Board of Institutional Care have also imposed limits, and the Swedish Enforcement Authority is reviewing the issue. ChatGPT and Claude now join DeepSeek on Sweden's list of unapproved AI tools.
report.impact: For the AI industry, Sweden's move reinforces that public-sector adoption depends on contracts, data residency, no-training guarantees, and audit trails, not just model quality. Vendors selling browser subscriptions without enterprise controls will struggle to win government clients, while Microsoft and providers offering sovereign or regulated deployments gain an edge. For developers, the lesson is to build administrative controls, logging, data-retention settings, and self-hosted options into AI products from the start. For regular users, the ban is a warning that consumer chatbots are not private workspaces; workplace use may increasingly shift to approved tools. It also signals that AI fragmentation by jurisdiction and sector is likely to grow.
report.tools: Readers following this issue should watch Microsoft 365 Copilot, which Sweden approved under a security agreement, and enterprise offerings from OpenAI and Anthropic that include data-processing terms and no-training options. For controlled or self-hosted deployments, open-source projects such as Ollama, Open WebUI, LibreChat, and LocalAI are worth exploring, though organizations must verify compliance, logging, and data-retention behavior before use.
